citation: Chicago Tribune, May 19, 1882, report of the Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to “The Old Settlers of Chicago”, held 18 May 1882, with the list “Names of Old Settlers Present, Residents and of Age Prior to 1840” and the speeches of Vice-President J. W. Doane and the Hon. John Wentworth.
describes_date: the reception of 1882-05-18; the guests' Chicago residence is placed only before 1840
locator: the roster “Names of Old Settlers Present, Residents and of Age Prior to 1840”, 128 printed entries from “Adams, William H., 451 Wabash avenue, Chicago” to “Yates, H. H., 19 South Peoria street, Chicago”, and the report's own counts
rights_note: Chicago Tribune, 1882: a United States imprint long out of copyright.
access_notes: READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, NOT AT THE PAGE — see chicagology_goldenage_063. THE PAGE'S DATELINES FOR TWO OF THESE DOCUMENTS READ 1892 AND THE DOCUMENTS ARE OF 1882. The page heads the Eells interview "Chicago Tribune, May 17, 1892" and the reception report "Chicago Tribune, May 19, 1892", and prints Eells's own bequest over the date "May 18, 1892". Six things inside the text put all three in 1882: the Tribune of 25 April 1882 announces the FOURTH annual reception for 18 May and the report calls itself the fourth; Eells says "I came here fifty years ago" of 1832; he gives his birth as 1814 and his age as 68; he says the razor-hone left with him "in Chicago in 1833" has been kept "forty-nine years"; he calls Gurdon S. Hubbard, born 1802, "over 80 years of age" and dines with him the next day, which no 1892 interview could do; and the death roll he shares the page with is Wentworth's list of 1881-82. The dates carried in these records are therefore 1882, and the page's own datelines are recorded here rather than followed.
what_it_supplies: 128 named men who were of age and living in Chicago before 1 January 1840, and where each of them lived in 1882
the club's own arithmetic of the settler population: 414 known old settlers, 35 dead in the year, 118 in the house, 160 at the third reception
a handful of trades and firsts attached to the year's dead — a Fort Dearborn gunsmith, the first grist-mill, the first mail rider to Milwaukee, the first frame building west of the river
what_it_does_not_supply: a year of arrival for any guest
an 1835 address: every address printed is of 1882
note: THE COUNT DISAGREES WITH THE LIST. The report says “there were in the house the following-named guests—118 in number” and the list under it carries 128 entries. Both numbers are recorded; neither is corrected.
